title: His will as yours (Avot 2:4)
hook: make God's will your will, so God makes your will His

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabban Gamaliel paired Torah with derekh eretz, the work of the world. Your line was two hands, each keeping the other steady. Today, the same sage goes deeper.
screen: `TWO HANDS, EACH KEEPING THE OTHER STEADY.`

segments.voice: A kid cleans his room because he's told to. Years later, grown up, he cleans it because he actually likes a clean room. Same broom, same floor. But something changed inside: the rule stopped being someone else's and became his. That shift, from have to, to want to, is what today's saying is about. It's a bold line, and it talks about God's will and yours as if they could become the same thing.
screen: `TOLD TO CLEAN THE ROOM.` → `WANTING A CLEAN ROOM.` → `FROM HAVE TO, TO WANT TO.`

segments.voice: Rabban Gamaliel, son of Rabbi Judah, says this. Do His will as if it were your will, so that He will do your will as if it were His. Set aside your will before His will, so that He will set aside the will of others before yours. The Hebrew for will is ratzon: what you want, what pleases you, your desire. The saying is built like a mirror, your will and God's reflected back and forth. Commentators read it more than one way. Some take it practically: spend on doing good as gladly as you spend on what you want for yourself, and good things will come back to you. Others hear something inward. At first a commandment feels like someone else's rule. Over years of doing it, you can come to want it, the way the kid comes to want the clean room. Then what God wants and what you want aren't two different things anymore. The second half is harder. Sometimes what you want and what's good really do pull apart, and the saying asks you to let the good win. It doesn't promise you'll always get your way. It speaks of God setting aside the will of others, the pressure and plans of people around you, on your behalf. So the carry is simple: want what's good. And it closes a week of sayings: someone else's share was in the pile, silence, truth, justice and peace, it will be well with you, Malachi's book, two hands, each keeping the other steady, and today, his will as yours.
screen: `RATZON: WHAT YOU WANT.` · `A SAYING BUILT LIKE A MIRROR.` · `FROM HAVE TO, TO WANT TO.` · `SET YOUR WILL ASIDE.` · then, large: `WANT WHAT'S GOOD.`

segments.voice: Let one strong want come up, a thing, a result, someone's approval, and look at it honestly without pushing it away. Is there a good version inside it? Wanting money might hide wanting to care for someone; wanting to win might hide wanting to be seen. Let the wish lean toward that good thing, and if you pray, you can offer it to God.
Ratzon. Will, what you want: the word behind Rabban Gamaliel's mirror, do God's will as if it were your own.
Your line: want what's good. Have to can grow into want to. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Jewish teachers describe growth in observance as moving from doing a commandment because it is commanded to doing it with love, and this saying is studied as a picture of that change.

fork.setup: you do a good thing every week, but only because you have to. what does Rabban Gamaliel's saying hope for?
options: that you stop, since your heart isn't in it.
that over time you come to want it.
that you keep doing it and never mind why.

chat.says: Does 'do God's will as if it were yours' mean you'll always get what you want?
options: No. Over time, have to can grow into want to, until you want what's good.
Yes. Keep the commandments and every wish you have is sure to come true.
No. It means you only need to keep the commandments you already like.
chat.meaning: The saying doesn't promise you'll get your way. Commentators hear a slow change: a rule becomes your own, until you want what's good.

notes: Avot is paraphrased (outline follows Taylor 1897). In some editions this saying is numbered 2:4, in others it falls in 2:3–4.
The practical reading (spend on mitzvot as on your own desires) is attributed to Bartenura and others; confirm.
The inward reading (from obligation to love) is a general interpretive framing; confirm it is fair.
